title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Alternating
description:
# Minimum Operations to Make Array Alternating

You are given an integer array `nums`. In one operation, you may change any one element to any positive integer.

An array is alternating when both conditions hold:

* every pair of adjacent elements has different values;
* every pair of elements with the same parity index has the same value. In other words, all even indices share one value and all odd indices share one value.

Return the minimum number of operations needed to make `nums` alternating.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [3,1,3,2,4,3]
**Output:** 3
**Explanation:** Keep value `3` on even indices and value `1` on odd indices. Three positions must change.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,2,2,2]
**Output:** 2
**Explanation:** Value `2` is most frequent on both parities, so one side must use its second-best choice or a new value.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10^5`
* `1 <= nums[i] <= 10^5`

solutions.name: HashMap Top Two by Parity
solutions.description:
## Approach

Count value frequencies separately for even indices and odd indices using hash maps. Extract the top two values from each parity and try the four possible top-pair combinations, keeping only pairs whose values differ.

## Key Insight

For each parity, only the two most frequent values can matter. If the best even value and best odd value differ, they are optimal. If they conflict, one side must give up its best value, so the answer is determined by pairing a best value with the other side's second-best value.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Counting Array Top Two
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the constraint `nums[i] <= 100000` directly. Build two frequency arrays, one for even indices and one for odd indices, then extract the top two values from each array and choose the best non-conflicting pair.

## Key Insight

The value domain is bounded, so a dense counting array can replace hash maps. The optimization target is still the same: maximize kept positions under the requirement that the even value and odd value are different.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n + U)
- Space Complexity: O(U)

solutions.name: Explicit Conflict Formula
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute the top two frequency choices for both parity groups. If the two best values are different, keep both. If they are the same, compare the two legal repairs: keep the best even value with the second-best odd value, or keep the second-best even value with the best odd value.

## Key Insight

There is only one possible conflict: both parities want the same most frequent value. In that case, changing one parity away from its best value is unavoidable, and the better of the two second-choice repairs is globally optimal.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Sorted Frequency Candidate Lists
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build frequency maps for both parities, turn each map into a list of candidates sorted by descending count, and scan for the best pair with different values. Sentinels with count zero represent changing an entire parity group to a new value when no existing value is legal.

## Key Insight

Sorting makes the greedy search transparent: for a fixed even-side choice, the first odd candidate with a different value is the best possible odd partner. Once the best possible remaining pair cannot beat the current answer, the scan can stop.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n + u log u)
- Space Complexity: O(u)

solutions.name: Asymmetric Best-Partner Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute frequency maps and the top two candidates for each parity. Enumerate every value that might be kept on one side, and pair it with the best candidate from the other side that does not use the same value. Do this from both directions to include cases where one parity keeps no existing value.

## Key Insight

The expensive part is not choosing both values; it is knowing the best legal partner for a chosen value. The other parity's top two candidates are enough to answer that partner query in constant time.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n + u)
- Space Complexity: O(u)
